summary: Specifies explicit subscriptions for the SIP REFER method. REFER creates an implicit event subscription, which complicates negotiating extensions and avoiding dialog sharing, so this document lets a subscription be set up separately.

eli5.summary: Asking a friend to pass a message used to also sign you up for updates by default. Now signing up is its own clear step.

questions: what is the sip refer explicitsub option tag
what is the nosub option tag
subtitle: Lets a SIP REFER skip its built-in subscription, and optionally swap in a normal SUBSCRIBE of the caller's choosing.

tldr.problem: A SIP REFER request silently creates an implicit event subscription. That blocks the normal tools for negotiating subscriptions and extensions, and it causes dialog reuse when REFER is sent inside an INVITE dialog.
tldr.mechanism: Two option tags go in the Require header of a REFER. 'explicitsub' removes the implicit subscription and returns a Refer-Events-At URI that the sender can SUBSCRIBE to. 'nosub' removes it and says no subscription will follow.
tldr.outcome: REFER can be used inside an existing dialog without dialog reuse, and refer subscriptions can use ordinary SUBSCRIBE negotiation. It updates RFC 3515 and is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 7614 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2015. It has not been obsoleted or updated, and it updates RFC 3515.

sections.title: Why the Implicit Subscription Is a Problem
sections.content:
The SIP REFER request, defined in RFC 3515, asks another party to contact a resource, as in call transfer. Sending it also triggers an implicit subscription to the 'refer' event, so the sender receives NOTIFY messages about how the referred request is going.

The RFC names two difficulties. First, sending REFER inside a dialog created by an INVITE reuses that dialog, with the problems described in RFC 5057. The SIP event framework in RFC 6665 disallows such reuse, so call transfer in RFC 5589 has to send REFER on a new dialog and tie it to the old one with the 'Target-Dialog' mechanism of RFC 4538.

Second, because there is no explicit SUBSCRIBE, subscription duration and Event header parameters cannot be negotiated. The Supported and Require extension mechanisms also become unclear: it is not obvious whether an extension applies to the REFER itself, to the subscription it creates, or to both.
sections.eli5: When you ask someone to pass a note, you get signed up for updates without being asked. That makes it hard to agree on how often updates come, or to keep the note passing and the updates separate.

sections.title: Two Extensions, Two Option Tags
sections.content:
The document defines two mechanisms that remove the implicit subscription. Either may be used within an existing dialog or out of dialog, because neither can create a new usage inside a dialog. The benefits listed are: REFER inside INVITE-created dialogs without dialog reuse, standard subscription parameter negotiation, and standard negotiation of SIP extensions.

  • explicitsub: no implicit subscription, but the sender may subscribe explicitly later.
  • nosub: no implicit subscription, and the sender tells the recipient that no explicit subscription will be forthcoming.

The sender puts the chosen tag in the Require header field of the REFER. A recipient that does not support or will not use the extension answers with a 420 (Bad Extension) response, and the sender can retry without the extension.
sections.eli5: There are two buttons. One says 'I will sign up for updates myself, tell me where'. The other says 'no updates needed, do not even set anything up'.

sections.title: How Explicit Subscriptions Work
sections.content:
A sender that includes explicitsub forms the REFER as in RFC 3515. The recipient uses its usual admission policy. It MUST NOT create an implicit subscription, and accepting the request does not create a dialog or a new usage in an existing one. The requirements of RFC 6665, such as providing a GRUU as local contact, do not apply to the accepting message unless the element would be a notifier in that dialog for some other reason.

A recipient that accepts MUST return a 200 response with a Refer-Events-At header field holding a sip: or sips: URI. That URI must uniquely identify this refer event state and must reach the event server when used in a SUBSCRIBE from the sender. The event server is often the recipient itself, but the extension also allows it to be a separate element fed by mechanisms such as PUBLISH (RFC 3903), and it allows more than one subscription to the same state.

The sender, if it cares about the outcome, then sends a SUBSCRIBE following RFC 6665, with the token 'refer' in the Event header and the URI in the Request-URI. It MUST NOT reuse any existing dialog identifiers. The server sends an immediate NOTIFY with the current state, more NOTIFYs as it changes, and a terminal NOTIFY at the end; the first NOTIFY may also be the last. Later SUBSCRIBE requests to refresh or end the subscription must carry the id parameter from the NOTIFY Event header, even though the unique URI makes it redundant. The RFC keeps that rule to minimise changes to existing implementations and diagnostic tools.

Forking matters. Only one final response reaches the sender, so if the REFER could be accepted in several places and the sender must learn about each, 'explicitsub' is not appropriate. Sending in an existing dialog or using Target-Dialog avoids this.
sections.eli5: You hand over your note and get a claim ticket with a one-of-a-kind address on it. Whenever you like, you go to that address and ask how it is going.

sections.title: Keeping the Refer State Around
sections.content:
With an implicit subscription, an implementation could throw away the refer event state right after the terminating NOTIFY. That is no longer safe. The referred request can finish before the REFER response reaches the sender and before the sender's SUBSCRIBE arrives.

So the event server MUST keep the final refer event state for a reasonable period, which SHOULD be at least 2*64*T1 (64 seconds), an upper-bound estimate of two non-INVITE transactions: the REFER and an immediate SUBSCRIBE. A SUBSCRIBE that arrives in that window is accepted and immediately terminated with a NOTIFY carrying the final state, with Subscription-State terminated and reason 'noresource'. A SUBSCRIBE might also never arrive.

Implementations should have the event server ready before sending the REFER response, but still send the response as soon as possible, as for all non-INVITE responses (RFC 4321).
sections.eli5: If the errand finishes before you come to ask, the answer has to stay on the counter for a while, so you still find out how it went.

sections.title: Refer-Events-At and the 'nosub' Rules
sections.content:
Refer-Events-At is an extension header defined with ABNF (RFC 5234): the header name, a SIP-URI or SIPS-URI in mandatory angle brackets, then optional generic parameters. A bare URI without the brackets is invalid. It is only meaningful in a 2xx response to a REFER; anywhere else it MUST be ignored.

For nosub, the sender tells the recipient it will not subscribe. The recipient follows its normal admission policy, creates no implicit subscription, and is not required to keep any state for refer event subscriptions. It still processes the Refer-To request as in RFC 3515, but saves the cost of preparing for subscribers.

Both tags may be used in a Require header only in a REFER request, or in a 200 or 421 response to one. They may also appear in Supported and in the sip.extensions feature tag (RFC 3840), which only signals awareness. A server must not put a tag in the Require of a 200 unless the request had it. A server that sees one of them in Supported and wants it returns a 421 response naming the required extension.
sections.eli5: The address on the claim ticket must be written in a strict way, with the pointy brackets. And if you say 'no updates', the other side does not bother keeping any records for you.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Everything in RFC 3515 still applies. The new issue is authorization. Before, only the element that sent the REFER could subscribe; now there may be several subscribers. An event server may accept an initial SUBSCRIBE because its Request-URI matches existing refer event state. Anyone holding that URI is effectively authorized, so the URI should be hard to guess (a temporary GRUU is one good way) and should be protected in transit, for example with TLS or DTLS (RFC 3261). Using only sips: URIs is a good way to force a protected transport. The server can demand more authorization, such as an identity assertion per RFC 4474.

A malicious sender could choose the Refer-Events-At URI to aim a SUBSCRIBE at a victim as raw traffic. Over UDP to a non-SIP host, retransmissions give at most a factor of 11 amplification. The RFC rates the risk lower than for the Refer-To URI, since the URI can only be sip: or sips: and appears only in a REFER response.
sections.eli5: Whoever knows the secret claim-ticket address can ask about your errand, so the address must be hard to guess and carried in a sealed envelope.

sections.title: Changes to RFC 3515 and IANA Registrations
sections.content:
The document updates RFC 3515. The old requirement in its Section 2.4.4 to reject out-of-dialog SUBSCRIBE requests for event 'refer' is removed. An element MAY accept such a SUBSCRIBE, so REFER is no longer the only way to create a subscription to that event.

IANA registered the 'explicitsub' and 'nosub' option tags in the SIP Option Tags subregistry, and the Refer-Events-At header field (compact form: none) in the SIP Header Fields subregistry.
sections.eli5: An old rule that said 'only the note passer may ask about progress' was dropped, and the new names were written in the official list.
